Appending a line counts as SENT; the gateway sends every line in that file.", "file": "notifications/sms.py"}, {"id": "R2", "statement": "The outbox record format in data/outbox/sms.jsonl is one JSON object per line with keys: id (e.g. 'SMS-00001'), household_id (e.g. 'HH-10170'), phone, template_id ('DELIVERY_DAY'), params ({'site': ..., 'day': ...}), text, queued_at. Note send_sms() itself only writes id/phone/text/queued_at; the existing outbox lines also carry household_id, template_id and params, so a resend script that wants 'same details' must copy those fields itself.", "file": "data/outbox/sms.jsonl"}, {"id": "R3", "statement": "delivery_status() -> dict[str, str] reads data/sms_status.json, mapping SMS ID to 'delivered' or 'failed'. Both are reusable helpers.", "file": "notifications/sms.py"}, {"id": "R4", "statement": "Current gateway status: failed = SMS-00002, SMS-00005, SMS-00007, SMS-00008, SMS-00010, SMS-00012, SMS-00013, SMS-00014, SMS-00015 (9 messages); the rest are delivered. These 9 failed messages belong to households HH-10332, HH-11169, HH-13498, HH-13919, HH-14133, HH-14923, HH-15407, HH-16705, HH-16888 — each household appears exactly once, so resending per failed message texts each household exactly once.", "file": "data/sms_status.json"}, {"id": "R5", "statement": "New SMS IDs are generated with format_sms_id(next_number([m['id'] for m in sent_messages()], 'SMS-'), ...): format_sms_id(number) -> 'SMS-{number:05d}' and next_number(existing_ids, prefix) returns 1 + the highest number used with that prefix.
